analysis.title: Doing The Fed's Work: Michael Wilson Says Tighter Financial Conditions Have Already Crushed The Average Stock... Just Not The Index
key_insights: Morgan Stanley's Wilson argues weak breadth in economically sensitive areas shows tighter financial conditions across rates, the dollar and oil are already doing part of the Fed's work. Index-level weakness is absent because the largest AI-centric weights are less sensitive to oil and cost of capital.

Morgan Stanley's financial conditions composite (52-week z-score averaged across rates, dollar and energy) is about 1.4 standard deviations, a level breached only a handful of times in 35 years, most recently in 2022.
The FOMC hiked 25bps to 3.75-4.00% last month. Warsh cited stronger labor and activity data, sticky inflation and geopolitics' effect on commodities. Goldman now pencils in a second hike in October.

Of the roughly 130bp rise in the 10-year since February, about 120bp came through real yields. Equities have historically absorbed breakeven-led rises more easily than real-yield-led ones, which explains the sharply negative stock/yield correlation.

Wilson says the risk is less the level of yields than the pace of the move. Another real-yield-led spike in bond volatility would be the more challenging outcome. 10Y above 5% is not outrageous with trailing 10-year nominal GDP growth near 6%.
The S&P 500 Equal-Weight Index has lagged cap-weight by 6% over six months. In September, when the 10-year moved above 5%, equal-weight fell 5% while cap-weight was roughly flat.

Over the trailing 30 days only TMT and Energy are positive among S&P sectors. Healthcare -3.5%, Consumer Discretionary -3.6%, Utilities -4.6%, Industrials -5.8%, Financials -7.7%, Materials -7.9%, REITs -9.8%.
85% of S&P 500 names are more than 10% below their all-time highs, 59% more than 20% below, 41% more than 30% below, 26% more than 40% below and 17% more than 50% below, per a ZeroHedge count.

Wilson's breadth gauge: the share of S&P members above their 200-day moving average fell to 43% at end of September, below the late-March low of 44%, then recovered to 50%. Forward P/E retested its March low near 19x.

Wilson reads the de-rating as having run ahead of any earnings deterioration, a classic mid-cycle combination. His equity risk premium framework puts fair value near 19.6x versus 19.2x today, so equities do not need a large bond rally if yields consolidate.

ZeroHedge notes that the S&P 500 equity risk premium (forward earnings yield minus the 10Y) is below zero, a level barely visited since 2002. Stocks are cheap against a model assuming yields stop rising and expensive against rising bond yields.

Wilson does not yet see higher yields migrating into a growth problem: nominal GDP printed 8.5%, median stock earnings growth is mid-teens, fed funds less core CPI is about 1.4%, and 10s2s is about +45bp. He says it is rare to see growth deterioration within 12-18 months under these conditions.

Wilson's two tells are relative performance of Financials, which he calls perhaps the most important for near-term equity direction, and bond volatility (MOVE index). Both show some stabilization but need more follow-through. MOVE surged above 110 in late September.
Goldman's Privorotsky observed that longer-dated bond vols have retraced roughly 30% of their recent move.
Upcoming tests: September CPI on Wednesday (consensus headline +0.6% MoM on a 9.6% gasoline jump, annual rate 3.6%), Warsh's IMF fireside chat Thursday, and the October 28 FOMC.

Goldman's Pasquariello pushes back on the breadth concern: the median S&P stock is 15% below its 52-week high, the worst since the dot-com bubble, but major US indices are up double digits YTD, all but two sectors are higher, and nearly 2 in 3 S&P names are positive. 123 names are up 25% or more versus 42 down 25% or more.

Pasquariello says positioning is light: GS sentiment indicator negative six straight weeks, GS prime book net exposure in the 10th percentile of the past year, and client turnover on last week's breakout ranked 49th of 52 weeks. He recommends staying short fixed income and long NDX, and flags 2027 as complicated, with lockup expirations potentially lifting net US equity supply the most since 2000.

Wilson's conclusion is unchanged: stay with quality but broaden, adding risk through higher-quality cyclicals. Capital Goods stands out, with revisions breadth improving from 16% in February to nearly 40%. His bullish base case carries an 8,300 S&P target.
ZeroHedge's own view is that the bearish path (real yields spike, bond vol re-erupts, index catches down to members) is more likely than Wilson's base case.

sector_views.rationale: Morgan Stanley remains overweight Financials. Wilson says Financials stabilizing is the key near-term signal before an all-clear on index catch-down. Sector is down 7.7% in 30 days and near its lowest relative level to the S&P since at least 2019.
Wilson favors higher-quality cyclicals. Revisions breadth improved from 16% in February to nearly 40% as manufacturing backlogs broaden across machinery and fabricated metals.

earnings_insights: Wilson says median stock earnings growth is running in the mid-teens, and the valuation de-rating has run well ahead of any deterioration in earnings.
Big banks kick off earnings season the Monday after this note (Oct 19).

macro_indicators.interpretation: About 120bp of the roughly 130bp rise since February came from real yields, which weighs more on equities than breakeven-led rises.
Goldman expects a second hike in October. Fed funds less core CPI is about 1.4%.
Supports Wilson's view that 10Y yields above 5% are consistent with growth. Trailing 10-year nominal GDP is near 6%.

macro_indicators.reading: +0.6% consensus, driven by a 9.6% gasoline rise
macro_indicators.interpretation: A measured headline print is implausible per ZeroHedge. A hot print would add pressure on policy-rate expectations and the long end.
Lifts the annual rate. Core is expected to be more measured.
Positively sloped, with the 2-year about 90bp above fed funds. Wilson sees this as a condition against near-term growth deterioration.
Contingent on Warsh blinking, yields consolidating and Financials turning.

trade_ideas.description: Stay short fixed income, stay long NDX
trade_ideas.rationale: Pasquariello bets the bond market keeps tightening financial conditions while AI-heavy mega caps ignore it.

trade_ideas.description: Add risk through higher-quality cyclicals, particularly Capital Goods, rather than moving down in quality
trade_ideas.rationale: Earnings remain strong, rates sticky, and revisions breadth in Capital Goods improved to nearly 40% from 16%.
trade_ideas.risk: Real-yield-led spike in bond vol would pull the index down toward breadth.

risk_factors: Another real-yield-led spike in bond volatility.
Hot September CPI driven by gasoline, and a Fed that has not signaled it sees tighter conditions as doing its work.
Higher yields migrating from a valuation problem into a growth problem.
S&P equity risk premium below zero, a level last seen around 2002.
Financials failing to stabilize in earnings season.
2027 equity supply from lockup expirations potentially the largest since 2000.
vol_and_positioning: MOVE index surged above 110 in late September as Treasury vol decoupled from a low VIX.
Longer-dated bond vols have retraced roughly 30% of their recent move (Goldman's Privorotsky).
Goldman sentiment indicator negative six straight weeks. GS prime book net exposure in the 10th percentile of the past year. Client turnover ranked 49th of 52 weeks on last week's S&P breakout.
Friday's session traded on the lowest volume in 23 years.
Share of S&P members above their 200-day moving average was 43% at end of September, 50% after recovering.
geopolitical: Geopolitics cited by Warsh as a driver of higher commodity prices and long-end yields, with oil elevated.
cross_bank_references: Goldman's Pasquariello pushes back on the breadth concern raised by Morgan Stanley's Wilson: 'I'm not sure that conditions are as dire as they're reported to be.'
Pasquariello's 'stay short fixed income; stay long NDX' is described as a twist Wilson won't love, since it bets on the divergence Wilson says must be resolved.
Goldman penciled in a second Fed hike in October after the September hike.

tension_points.bull_case: Wilson's base case: Warsh blinks, yields consolidate, Financials turn and the average stock catches up, with an 8,300 S&P target. Valuation is near fair value (19.2x vs 19.6x), earnings are mid-teens for the median stock and nominal GDP is 8.5%.
tension_points.bear_case: Real yields spike again, bond vol re-erupts and the index catches down to its members. The equity risk premium is below zero and a hot gasoline-driven CPI is expected.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Financials failing to stabilize in bank earnings, or another real-yield-led spike in bond volatility (MOVE back above its late-September 110 level).

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman's Pasquariello: major indices are up double digits YTD, nearly 2 in 3 S&P names are positive, and 123 names are up 25%+ versus 42 down 25%+. Positioning is light, so there is room for chase.
tension_points.bear_case: Median S&P stock is 15% below its 52-week high, the worst since the dot-com bubble. 85% of names are more than 10% below all-time highs and 17% are in 50%+ drawdowns.
